Well, doctor, it is... gosh, it is just so much all at once. But I guess what really brings me in, what finally made me pick up the phone and make the appointment, is that I feel like I am constantly running on a motor lately. I mean, just constantly, from the second I wake up. 

I am a special education teacher, and you know, that takes a lot of energy on a good day, but it is like I finish one thing at school—whether it is an evaluation meeting or getting the kids settled or sorting out the classroom materials—and I immediately jump right into the next thing. And you would think at 58 years old I would be slowing down a bit, maybe sitting in the staff room for five minutes between periods, but I just cannot do it.

I walk through the front door and I am immediately fixing a loose hinge in the garage, and then before I even put the tools away I am in the kitchen scrubbing the counters, and then I am out in the yard pulling weeds. I just jump from task to task to task without ever being able to shut myself off. It is like the off-switch is completely broken. My family tells me to just sit down and relax for ten minutes, but if I try to sit in the recliner in the evening, just to rest my bones, my whole body is just humming, pushing me to get back up and do something else. I just never, ever shut down.

So no, I definitely don't feel like I need less sleep, I honestly probably need a lot more! It is just that I cannot seem to make myself stop doing things long enough to actually get into the bed in the first place.

No, no, nothing like that. My wife—she's a remarkably light sleeper, bless her heart. I mean, if the neighbor's cat so much as walks across our front porch, she's sitting straight up in bed. Drowsy? Oh, gosh, no. No, no, no. I'm the exact opposite of drowsy. If anything, I honestly wish I could feel a little drowsy sometimes just to get a break from the motor, you know? ========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Recently? Oh, gosh, no. No, nothing like that. I'm actually healthy as a horse, thankfully. I mean, I go to my general practitioner—Dr. Henderson, he's over at that clinic on Elm Street, been seeing him for probably fifteen years now—and I just had my annual physical back in the fall. He always tells me my blood pressure is fantastic for a guy my age, which is honestly a miracle considering the stress of the education system these days. I don't take any daily medications, just a standard multivitamin in the morning with my coffee, and maybe an ibuprofen if my knees are barking after a long day of chasing kids around on those hard concrete floors at school. But no new prescriptions, no surgeries, no weird viruses or anything of the sort. 

But, well, the thing about your question is... you asked if anything changed around the time this started. The thing is, Doc, this didn't just *start*. This isn't some new development that popped up out of nowhere a few months ago. I've been like this... well, forever. Literally my whole life! My poor mother, rest her soul, she used to say I was born with a lawnmower engine attached to my backside. 

I can vividly remember being in third grade—Mrs. Gable's class, she was one of those old-school, incredibly strict teachers who would practically use a metronome to keep us in line—and she actually took a roll of masking tape and made a square on the floor around my desk. She told me I wasn't allowed to step outside the tape because I was just constantly up, wandering the aisles, checking the pencil sharpener, looking out the window, you name it. And even with the tape, I'd just stand inside that little square and bounce on my toes or drum my hands on the desk until she'd threaten to send me to the principal's office. 

So, no, it's not like I hit 58 and suddenly forgot how to sit in a chair. It's been my normal for as long as I can remember. I think maybe it's just... I don't know, maybe it feels more obvious now? Or maybe my wife is just getting less tolerant of it now that our own kids are grown and moved out. When the house was full of teenagers, my pacing and constantly fixing things blended right in with the general chaos of raising a family. Now that it's just the two of us in a quiet house, I think my inability to just sit on the couch and watch a movie with her for two hours is a lot more glaring. But medically? No changes at all. Just the same old me, running at a hundred miles an hour like always.

Well, see, that's the million-dollar question, isn't it? Because you're right, I've always had the motor. Always. Like I said about third grade, it's just who I am. But... was it always this *intense*? This exhausting? No. No, it wasn't.

I had space to let the engine run, I guess you could say. I was still moving constantly, but I was doing productive things with it, so I didn't feel this terribly wound up and drained by the end of the day. 

But this current level of trouble? This feeling like I'm just crawling out of my skin and completely exhausted by my own body? That's new. Well, relatively new. This specific level of trouble has been going on for about eight months now. 

And I know exactly why, too. About eight months ago, an older relative of ours—my wife's aunt, actually, Aunt Shirley, she's 82—she couldn't safely live on her own anymore, so she moved in with us. We put her in that guest room down the hall I was telling you about earlier. And, you know, don't get me wrong, I love Shirley, I really do. She's a sweet lady. But having her in the house has completely upended our entire ecosystem. 

She needs a lot of quiet, and she goes to bed incredibly early, like 6:30 or 7:00 in the evening. So all my usual ways of burning off this energy? Gone. I can't go down to the basement and run the table saw or hammer away at a project at 8 PM anymore because the noise echoes right up through the floorboards into her room. I can't pace the hallways because the hardwood floors creak, and she's a light sleeper, just like my wife. So after dinner, I'm basically confined to the living room armchair, and I'm supposed to just sit there and watch *Jeopardy* and *Wheel of Fortune* on low volume. 

It's like... imagine taking that lawnmower engine my mom talked about, and throwing a heavy, thick tarp over it while it's still running full blast. It's just overheating! I'm sitting in that chair, bouncing my leg, tapping my fingers, feeling the tension just build and build and build in my chest and my legs because I have nowhere to put all this physical energy. It is just draining the absolute life out of me. I've never felt this trapped by my own restlessness before. So, yeah, the constant moving has always been there, absolutely, but this unbearable, exhausting peak of it? That's strictly an eight-month development since Shirley took over the spare room and I lost my ability to just roam around my own house.

I just jump from task to task to task without ever being able to shut myself off. It is like the off-switch is completely broken. My family tells me to just sit down and relax for ten minutes, but if I try to sit in the recliner in the evening, just to rest my bones, my whole body is just humming, pushing me to get back up and do something else. I just never, ever shut down.\n\nDoctor: When you say you're constantly running on this motor, how many hours of sleep are you actually getting at night? And do you feel rested, or do you feel like you need less sleep than you used to?\n\nPatient: Sleep? Well, it is not that I feel like I *need* less sleep, if that makes sense. It is not like I am one of those people who can just sleep for three hours and wake up feeling like a million bucks. No, no, I am bone tired. I mean, you can imagine, chasing after middle schoolers with severe behavioral needs all day, and then doing yard work until the sun goes down... I am physically exhausted. My joints ache. \n\nBut when I finally do try to get into bed—and getting into bed is a whole elaborate process, let me tell you, because I will go to brush my teeth and suddenly realize the bathroom sink needs scrubbing, and then before I know it I am organizing the entire medicine cabinet at 11:30 at night while my wife is just begging me to please turn off the light and come to bed—but when I finally do lay down, I don't feel rested at all. \n\nAs for exactly how many hours I am actually getting, gosh, I don't even really know. I don't keep track of the exact numbers. I guess once I finally, truly crash and burn for the night, I probably sleep a normal amount? I am not really sure. But I definitely never wake up feeling refreshed or rejuvenated. I wake up and... boom, the motor is just running again. My feet hit the floor and I am instantly thinking about the IEP meetings I have that day, and whether I need to mow the lawn before it rains on Thursday, and I am just instantly off to the races again. So no, I definitely don't feel like I need less sleep, I honestly probably need a lot more! It is just that I cannot seem to make myself stop doing things long enough to actually get into the bed in the first place.\n\nDoctor: During these times when you feel this motor running and you're jumping from task to task, do you ever experience sudden episodes where your heart races, you feel short of breath, or you have a sense of panic or dread—or is it more of a constant restless drive without those acute episodes?\n\nPatient: No, no, it's nothing like that. I don't get those... what did you call them, acute episodes? No, my heart isn't pounding out of my chest like I'm having a heart attack or something, and I don't feel like I can't breathe. It's not a panic thing. I don't feel dread, really. I mean, I might feel stressed about all the paperwork I have to do—because, let me tell you, the amount of paperwork they expect from special ed teachers these days is just astronomical, it's a mountain of forms for every single student, and if you miss one signature the whole district gets in an uproar—but it's not a sudden panic attack. \n\nIt's really just exactly what you said, that constant restless drive. It's just this hum in my bones. Like yesterday, for example, I was trying to watch a movie with my wife—she loves those historical dramas, the ones that are three hours long and very slow-paced—and I was sitting there on the couch, and I wasn't panicked, I wasn't short of breath, but my leg was bouncing, and my fingers were drumming on the armrest, and all I could think about was the fact that the gutters really need cleaning before the autumn leaves start falling in earnest. And I kept trying to focus on the movie, but the physical urge to just get up and get the ladder out of the shed was so overwhelming. I ended up getting up and reorganizing the Tupperware drawer while watching from the kitchen doorway. So it's not fear or panic, it's just... I just have to be moving. I have to be doing something. It never spikes into terror, it just stays at this constant, exhausting level of 'go, go, go.'\n\nDoctor: When you're experiencing this constant motor drive and restlessness, do you find yourself worrying a lot—like, is your mind racing with anxious thoughts about things that might go wrong, or is it more that your body just won't settle down while your mind might be relatively calm?\n\nPatient: Well, it's... it's definitely not worry, not in the sense of being anxious about things going wrong. I'm not sitting there chewing my fingernails worrying that the house is going to burn down or that I'm going to lose my job or anything like that. It's not a fearful racing mind. I mean, sure, I have the normal stresses, like I mentioned with the paperwork, or worrying if one of my students is going to have a meltdown during an assembly, which, believe me, happens more often than you'd think and requires a whole protocol to handle. But that's just normal teacher stuff, you know? It's not this paralyzing, anxious worry.\n\nMy mind *is* racing, though, but it's racing with... with tasks. With things to do. It's like a running to-do list that just never ends and keeps scrolling and scrolling in my head. Like I said about the gutters, right? I wasn't *worried* the gutters were going to cause a flood and destroy the foundation of the house, I just couldn't stop thinking about the physical act of cleaning them. It's like my brain is a pinball machine, and the ball is just bouncing from \"fix the hinge\" to \"grade the math worksheets\" to \"clean the Tupperware drawer\" to \"mow the lawn.\" \n\nSo my mind isn't calm, exactly, because it's always plotting the next five things I need to physically do, but it's not anxious. It's just... driven. And my body is just following along, or maybe my body is driving the brain, I don't even know which comes first anymore! It's just this physical inability to settle. My wife will say, \"Just turn your brain off for a minute,\" and I try to explain to her that it's not like I'm sitting there fretting over the state of the world, I'm just physically incapable of sitting still when my brain is telling me there are fourteen things in the garage that need organizing right this very second. So no, it's not anxious worry, it's just this overwhelming urge to be doing, doing, doing, all the time.\n\nDoctor: Has your wife or anyone else ever noticed you stop breathing during the night, or gasp or choke in your sleep? Or do you ever wake up gasping for air?\n\nPatient: No, no, nothing like that. My wife—she's a remarkably light sleeper, bless her heart. I mean, if the neighbor's cat so much as walks across our front porch, she's sitting straight up in bed. So she would absolutely notice if I stopped breathing or started choking or gasping in the middle of the night. She's never mentioned anything of the sort. \n\nWhat she *does* mention, and honestly she brings it up at least twice a week, is how much I toss and turn. Because even when I'm asleep, I guess I'm still moving. I'm kicking the sheets, flipping over, adjusting the pillows... we actually had to upgrade to a king-size mattress about five years ago, because when we had the queen, I was practically knocking her off the edge with all my thrashing around. And even with the extra space, she still threatens to send me to the guest room down the hall sometimes just so she can get some peace! \n\nBut as far as my breathing goes? No, perfectly normal. I never wake up gasping for air or feeling choked. Like I said before, when I wake up, I just wake up instantly wide awake and ready to go, thinking about lesson plans or whether I need to change the oil in the lawnmower. There's no choking or struggling to breathe at all, just a whole lot of restless kicking.\n\nDoctor: During the day, do you find yourself feeling excessively drowsy or struggling to stay awake, even though you're constantly moving around and doing things? For example, do you ever nod off unintentionally during the day, like while driving or sitting at your desk?\n\nPatient: Drowsy? Oh, gosh, no. No, no, no. I'm the exact opposite of drowsy. If anything, I honestly wish I could feel a little drowsy sometimes just to get a break from the motor, you know? It might be nice to just sit in a chair and actually feel relaxed enough to let my eyes drift shut, but that just doesn't happen for me. \n\nI mean, if you think about my day... I'm a special ed teacher, so from the moment that first bell rings at 7:45 AM, I am on my feet. And even when I do have a prep period—which is supposed to be my 45 minutes of quiet time sitting at my desk grading or doing all that IEP paperwork I was telling you about—I'm absolutely not nodding off. I can't even sit in the chair properly! I'm usually pacing around the back of the classroom, or I'm standing up at the filing cabinet to read things, or I'm reorganizing the sensory bin for the third time that week. There's just no off switch. \n\nSometimes the other teachers in the breakroom—like Susan, the art teacher, she's always complaining about the 2 PM slump and drinking her third cup of coffee, and she'll ask me how I have so much energy. I always have to laugh because it doesn't feel like *good* energy, it's just that my body literally cannot stop moving. \n\nAnd you mentioned driving—never. I have a 40-minute commute each way, taking the interstate, and I am wide awake the entire time. I'm usually listening to an audiobook or the news, drumming my fingers on the steering wheel, thinking about what I'm going to make for dinner or what repairs the house needs. I don't ever get that heavy-eyelid feeling, not even a little bit. It's like my body doesn't know how to power down until I literally exhaust myself late at night, and even then, like I said about the bed, I'm still physically revved up and thrashing around. So, no, falling asleep at the wheel or nodding off at my desk? Never happens. I'm just running on this endless, exhausting supply of nervous energy all day long.\n\nDoctor: Have you had any major changes in your health recently—like a new diagnosis, a new medication you started taking, changes to an existing medication, or any kind of surgery or illness—around the time this constant motor and restlessness started?\n\nPatient: Recently? Oh, gosh, no. No, nothing like that. I'm actually healthy as a horse, thankfully. I mean, I go to my general practitioner—Dr. Henderson, he's over at that clinic on Elm Street, been seeing him for probably fifteen years now—and I just had my annual physical back in the fall. He always tells me my blood pressure is fantastic for a guy my age, which is honestly a miracle considering the stress of the education system these days. I don't take any daily medications, just a standard multivitamin in the morning with my coffee, and maybe an ibuprofen if my knees are barking after a long day of chasing kids around on those hard concrete floors at school. But no new prescriptions, no surgeries, no weird viruses or anything of the sort. \n\nBut, well, the thing about your question is... you asked if anything changed around the time this started. The thing is, Doc, this didn't just *start*. This isn't some new development that popped up out of nowhere a few months ago. I've been like this... well, forever. Literally my whole life! My poor mother, rest her soul, she used to say I was born with a lawnmower engine attached to my backside. \n\nI can vividly remember being in third grade—Mrs. Gable's class, she was one of those old-school, incredibly strict teachers who would practically use a metronome to keep us in line—and she actually took a roll of masking tape and made a square on the floor around my desk. She told me I wasn't allowed to step outside the tape because I was just constantly up, wandering the aisles, checking the pencil sharpener, looking out the window, you name it. It's been my normal for as long as I can remember. I think maybe it's just... I don't know, maybe it feels more obvious now? When the house was full of teenagers, my pacing and constantly fixing things blended right in with the general chaos of raising a family. Now that it's just the two of us in a quiet house, I think my inability to just sit on the couch and watch a movie with her for two hours is a lot more glaring. But medically? No changes at all. Just the same old me, running at a hundred miles an hour like always.\n\nDoctor: You mentioned this has been going on your whole life since third grade. No. No, it wasn't. \n\nI used to be able to channel it a lot better, I think. If you asked me five or ten years ago, I'd say I was just a really active guy. I'd come home from school, and if I couldn't sit still, I'd just go out to the garage and tinker with the lawnmower, or I'd reorganize the basement, or I'd take the dog for a long hike. I had... I had space to let the engine run, I guess you could say. I was still moving constantly, but I was doing productive things with it, so I didn't feel this terribly wound up and drained by the end of the day. \n\nBut this current level of trouble? This feeling like I'm just crawling out of my skin and completely exhausted by my own body? That's new. Well, relatively new. This specific level of trouble has been going on for about eight months now. \n\nAnd I know exactly why, too. About eight months ago, an older relative of ours—my wife's aunt, actually, Aunt Shirley, she's 82—she couldn't safely live on her own anymore, so she moved in with us. We put her in that guest room down the hall I was telling you about earlier. And, you know, don't get me wrong, I love Shirley, I really do. She's a sweet lady. But having her in the house has completely upended our entire ecosystem. \n\nShe needs a lot of quiet, and she goes to bed incredibly early, like 6:30 or 7:00 in the evening. I can't pace the hallways because the hardwood floors creak, and she's a light sleeper, just like my wife. It's just overheating! I'm sitting in that chair, bouncing my leg, tapping my fingers, feeling the tension just build and build and build in my chest and my legs because I have nowhere to put all this physical energy. It is just draining the absolute life out of me. I've never felt this trapped by my own restlessness before. Oh, it's definitely the physical part. My mind is sharp as a tack, honestly. I don't have any trouble at all focusing on the actual words on the page or losing my train of thought. It's entirely physical. My brain is perfectly willing to do the work, but my body just flat-out refuses to stay in the chair while I do it.

You've got your present levels of performance, the measurable annual goals, the accommodations, the behavioral intervention plans... it's a lot of legal jargon and data tracking. My brain was totally dialed into the task. I wasn't getting distracted by things out the window or forgetting what I was doing. 

The problem is just that my body won't cooperate with the physical act of sitting at the desk to type it out. I'll read a paragraph of the school psychologist's evaluation, and my brain is processing the information perfectly, but my legs are just... screaming to stand up. So I'll stand up. I'll take my laptop and set it on top of the tall filing cabinet near the door and type standing up for a minute. Then I'll pace to the back of the room while I think of how to phrase a specific math goal. And the whole time I'm pacing, I am completely focused on that math goal. I'm not jumping to a different task, I'm not losing my place. I'm just literally incapable of keeping my backside glued to the swivel chair. 

It's almost like my brain and my body are operating on two completely different wavelengths. The brain says, "Okay, let's sit and knock out this paperwork," and the body says, "Great idea, but let's do a marathon while we think about it." My wife used to ask me how I could grade thirty spelling tests while walking circles around the kitchen island, but for me, that's just how it works. The moving doesn't take my attention away from the task; I just have to be in constant motion while I do it. So, no, no issues with concentration or jumping around because I'm distracted. I just can't sit still to save my life.

I don't keep track of the exact numbers. I guess once I finally, truly crash and burn for the night, I probably sleep a normal amount? I am not really sure. I have a 40-minute commute each way, taking the interstate, and I am wide awake the entire time. So, no, falling asleep at the wheel or nodding off at my desk? Never happens. I'm just running on this endless, exhausting supply of nervous energy all day long.\n\nDoctor: Have you had any major changes in your health recently—like a new diagnosis, a new medication you started taking, changes to an existing medication, or any kind of surgery or illness—around the time this constant motor and restlessness started?\n\nPatient: Recently? My thyroid? You know, it's funny you ask about that, because my sister-in-law—my wife's sister, Brenda—she actually had a whole ordeal with her thyroid a few years back. I think hers was underactive? Well, no, it’s really just exactly like I was saying before—it's that pure, unadulterated urge to just... go. There’s absolutely no pain or weird sensations in the skin or the muscles themselves.

Five or ten minutes? Gosh, I... I honestly don't know if I could give you a straight answer on that. I'm really not sure, because I don't think I've ever actually made it that long to find out if it's strictly, you know, physically impossible.

Oh, well... no, having the basement to myself didn't make the motor stop. I mean, sure, it was absolutely wonderful having that space. When I was restoring that antique rocking chair—it was a really beautiful piece, solid oak, probably early 1900s, and I spent hours down there just sanding it, staining it, pacing around the workbench and working off some of that physical energy. But when I actually went upstairs and got into bed? The engine was still idling high. It always has been. 

Because, see, this isn't some new development just because Aunt Shirley moved in and hijacked the guest room and turned the hallway into an obstacle course. This is... this is just who I am. It's been a part of who I was long before adulthood, long before I ever met Linda or bought this house. This definitely isn't something that just started with this recent family change. 

In fact, my mother, God rest her soul, she used to always joke about it. She’d tell everyone at family gatherings that even back in elementary school, I practically taught the class from my seat. Or, well, I guess not *from* my seat, because the whole punchline was that I was *always* out of my chair. Constantly. Just wandering the aisles, looking at what the other kids were doing, or I'd be talking non-stop to whoever was unlucky enough to be sitting next to me. 

And the interrupting—oh, I was terrible about cutting in before the teacher even finished giving directions. Like, Mrs. Gable in third grade would be halfway through explaining a spelling worksheet, and I’d just blurt out the answer or ask what we were supposed to do next before she could even take a breath. My brain was just always ten steps ahead, and my body was right there with it, just completely unable to wait its turn. 

So, yeah, having the basement was a nice outlet, and losing it has definitely made things feel more... confined, I guess? Especially with all the oxygen tubes and boxes everywhere now. But that constant motor running inside me at night? That didn't just start eight months ago. That engine has been running on full throttle since I was a little kid in short pants. It's just always been there, buzzing away, whether I had a basement to pace around in or not.

It's just... it's exhausting trying to keep the whole machine in park when the engine is revving that high, and every single part of the car is vibrating because of it.\n\nDoctor: When you're sitting in that armchair at night and you feel the urge to move your legs, do you experience any uncomfortable sensations in your legs themselves—like tingling, crawling, burning, aching, or a sensation like something is moving under the skin—or is it purely a physical urge to move without any of those uncomfortable feelings?\n\nPatient: Well, no, it’s really just exactly like I was saying before—it's that pure, unadulterated urge to just... go. There’s absolutely no pain or weird sensations in the skin or the muscles themselves. \n\nLike I mentioned with my neighbor Tom and his whole \"bugs under the skin\" thing, I don't get anything even remotely close to that. No tingling, no crawling, no burning. It’s not an ache, either. I mean, I know what an ache feels like! I teach special ed in one of those modular portable classrooms out behind the main middle school building, and they just slapped this incredibly thin, cheap industrial carpet directly over a concrete slab. So after seven or eight hours of pacing around that room, redirecting kids and bending over their desks to help with math worksheets, my arches and my calves will legitimately ache from the concrete. I know that feeling well. \n\nBut what happens in the armchair at night is completely different. It’s not uncomfortable in a... in a sensory way, if that makes sense? I don't feel anything moving under my skin. It’s purely just this massive, undeniable physical command from my brain saying, \"We need to move. Right now.\" \n\nIt feels more like a coiled spring. You know when you wind up one of those little toy cars, the ones you pull back on the floor, and you can feel the tension in the gears just begging you to let go so it can shoot across the room? That’s what my legs feel like. That's what my whole body feels like, really. There's no burning, no numbness. If I try to ignore it and just force myself to sit there and watch the television, my legs don't start hurting or tingling... the urge just gets louder and louder and more impossible to ignore until I'm practically jumping out of the corduroy cushions. So, yeah, no weird nerve feelings or anything like that. Just... just a totally restless engine that's stuck in drive while my foot is slamming on the brake.\n\nDoctor: Has your wife ever mentioned that your leg movements at night follow a pattern—like, does she notice your legs kicking in a rhythmic, repetitive way, almost like you're pedaling a bicycle over and over, or is it more just random thrashing and shifting around?\n\nPatient: A bicycle? Oh, gosh, no, nothing as organized as that. I mean, if I were pedaling a bicycle in my sleep, Linda would probably be absolutely thrilled because at least it would be predictable, right? She could just, you know, stay out of the bike lane, so to speak! But no, she’s never mentioned anything about a rhythm or a pattern. It’s completely random. \n\nActually, I remember one morning—this was probably a couple of months ago, right before Shirley moved in and our whole routine got thrown out the window—Linda was sitting at the kitchen island with her coffee, just looking at me with these dark circles under her eyes, and she said, \"You were doing the spastic starfish again last night.\" That’s what she calls it! I might lay completely still for ten minutes—or at least she thinks I am—and then suddenly I’m launching my knee into the center of the mattress or throwing my arm over my head. \n\nSometimes she even tries to build this little barricade of pillows between us, just to absorb the shock of whatever random limb comes flying her way. I have zero control over it once I'm out.\n\nDoctor: When you're lying in bed and you feel that urge to move your legs, if you really tried hard to keep your legs completely still for, say, five or ten minutes, do you think you could hold them still if you concentrated on it, or is it physically impossible to resist the urge no matter how hard you try?\n\nPatient: Five or ten minutes? This definitely isn't something that just started with this recent family change. \n\nIn fact, my mother, God rest her soul, she used to always joke about it. Just wandering the aisles, looking at what the other kids were doing, or I'd be talking non-stop to whoever was unlucky enough to be sitting next to me. \n\nAnd the interrupting—oh, I was terrible about cutting in before the teacher even finished giving directions. Like, Mrs. Gable in third grade would be halfway through explaining a spelling worksheet, and I’d just blurt out the answer or ask what we were supposed to do next before she could even take a breath. My brain was just always ten steps ahead, and my body was right there with it, just completely unable to wait its turn. \n\nSo, yeah, having the basement was a nice outlet, and losing it has definitely made things feel more... confined, I guess?       "Symptoms not better explained by other medical conditions (thyroid, sleep apnea, restless legs syndrome all ruled out)",
      "Symptoms causing significant distress and impairment (exhaustion, marital stress, occupational difficulty managing evening time)",
      "No evidence of secondary anxiety disorder or panic disorder (symptoms are not fear-based)"
    ]
  }
}
